# Ray Casting with Depth/Alpha Test for Empty Space Skipping

Also called: Empty Space Skipping via OpenGL Tests, Ray Casting using Alpha and Depth Tests, Texture Slab Volume Rendering with GPU-based Acceleration, Westermann & Sevenich Empty Space Skipping, Westermann & Sevenich Technique

## Overview
This method accelerates ray-based volume rendering by using OpenGL’s alpha test and depth test to determine the near and far intersection points of rays with the volume, allowing samples to be taken only between these points [S3, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Space Leaping](5863-space-leaping.md) and [Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping](3852-occupancy-grid-and-map-based-empty-space-skipping.md) by performing the empty space detection entirely on the GPU using hardware z-occlusion culling, without requiring CPU-side preprocessing or [hierarchical data structures](#4133-hierarchical-data-structures.md) like octrees [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
The method relies on creating "Slab Silhouette Maps" (SSM) from [texture slabs](#7262-texture-slabs.md) to identify empty spaces and terminated rays, storing this information in the depth buffer [S1, unofficial]. The algorithm proceeds in three main phases: data preparation, silhouette map generation, and [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md).

### Inputs and Outputs
*   **Inputs:** 3D volume data (density/opacity), camera parameters (projection matrix $P$, modelview matrix $V$), and rendering parameters (number of samples $n$ per ray).
*   **Outputs:** Final color image in the framebuffer.

### Data Structures
1.  **Volume Data:** Stored as 2D texture slices. Slices are grouped into "texture slabs" [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Depth Buffer:** Used to store the near and far intersection distances in [normalized device coordinates](#842-ndc-ray-reparameterization.md) (NDC) [S3, unofficial].
3.  **[Display Lists](#2220-opengl-display-list-voxel-rendering.md):** Created for each set of textures (front-to-back and back-to-front) to optimize rendering order [S3, unofficial].

### Steps

1.  **Preprocessing (CPU):**
    *   Calculate the gradient of each volume element using central differences [S3, unofficial].
    *   Perform illumination and shading based on model variables and store the results in main memory [S3, unofficial]. [G: This step is specific to the implementation described in [S3, unofficial] where lighting is precomputed; other implementations may compute lighting per-sample on the GPU].

2.  **Texture Loading (GPU):**
    *   For each axis (X, Y, Z), create 2D textures for planes parallel to that axis [S3, unofficial].
    *   Load textures into GPU memory and create display lists for front-to-back and [back-to-front rendering](#2078-back-to-front-compositing.md) orders [S3, unofficial].

3.  **Camera Setup:**
    *   Determine the object axis with the smallest angle to the projection plane [S3, unofficial].
    *   Select the farthest texture from the camera in the selected axis set [S3, unofficial].
    *   Rotate the camera and draw textures starting from the selected one [S3, unofficial].

4.  **Silhouette Map Generation (Two Passes):**
    *   **Pass 1 (Near Points):**
        *   Initialize the depth buffer to 1.0 (maximum NDC value) [S3, unofficial].
        *   Set depth write criterion to `GL LESS` [S3, unofficial].
        *   Enable alpha test with `GL GREATER` and reference value $> 0$ to discard fragments with zero opacity [S3, unofficial].
        *   Render the volume slabs. This captures the distances of the closest significant fragments to the projection plane [S3, unofficial].
    *   **Pass 2 (Far Points):**
        *   Initialize the depth buffer to 0.0 (minimum NDC value) [S3, unofficial].
        *   Set depth write criterion to `GL GREATER` [S3, unofficial].
        *   Keep alpha test enabled [S3, unofficial].
        *   Render the volume slabs. This captures the distances of the farthest significant fragments from the projection plane [S3, unofficial].

5.  **Coordinate Conversion:**
    *   For each pixel $(X_s, Y_s, Z_s)$ in the depth buffer, convert NDC coordinates to world coordinates using the [inverse projection](#3162-pinhole-camera-projection-pixel-to-camera.md) and modelview matrices [S3, unofficial]:
        $$
        \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = (P M)^{-1} V \begin{bmatrix} X_s \\ Y_s \\ Z_s \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
        $$
    *   This yields the near point $P = (P_x, P_y, P_z)$ and far point $Q = (Q_x, Q_y, Q_z)$ [S3, unofficial].

6.  **Ray Casting and [Compositing](#2436-compositing.md):**
    *   For each pixel, cast a ray between $P$ and $Q$ [S3, unofficial].
    *   Sample the volume along the ray segment using parametric equations for $t \in [0, 1]$ with increment $1/n$:
        $$
        \begin{aligned}
        X(t) &= P_x + (Q_x - P_x)t \\
        Y(t) &= P_y + (Q_y - P_y)t \\
        Z(t) &= P_z + (Q_z - P_z)t
        \end{aligned}
        $$
    *   Composite the samples using the reduced volume rendering integral, skipping contributions from empty space (outside $P$ and $Q$) [S3, unofficial]:
        $$
        L(x) = \int_{x_A'}^{x_B'} \left[ e^{-\int_{x_A'}^{x_0} \phi_t(x')dx'} \epsilon(x_0) dx_0 \right]
        $$
        where $x_A'$ and $x_B'$ correspond to points $P$ and $Q$, $\phi_t$ is the extinction coefficient, and $\epsilon$ is the color [S3, unofficial].
    *   Draw the final color to the framebuffer [S3, unofficial].

### Parameters
*   **Alpha Test Reference Value:** $> 0$ [S3, unofficial].
*   **Number of Samples ($n$):** Determines the step size $1/n$ along the ray [S3, unofficial].

### Edge Cases and Pitfalls
*   **Coordinate System Mismatch:** The depth buffer uses NDC ([0,1]), but ray casting requires local volume or world coordinates. A transformation is necessary [S3, unofficial].
*   **High Data Dispersion:** If the volume has high dispersion (many internal empty spaces), the technique only skips external empty spaces, reducing effectiveness [S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Impostor Depth Optimization](4434-impostor-depth-optimization.md)
[Impostor Depth Optimization](#4434-impostor-depth-optimization.md) is a rendering [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) technique that uses camera-facing quads placed at the nearest point of volumetric primitives (such as spheres) to leverage the GPU's depth test for early culling. It solves the performance bottleneck in deep piles of overlapping objects where full shading (including ray tracing) is prohibitively expensive. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by replacing per-object [ray-volume intersection](#2381-ray-volume-intersection-face-distance-method.md) logic with a fixed-screen-space primitive that triggers hardware depth discard, effectively skipping the fragment shader for occluded layers.

### Polygon Assisted Ray Casting
Polygon Assisted Ray Casting (PARC) is an optimization for primary rays in volumetric ray tracing using graphics hardware. It creates a polygonal representation of all objects and projects them into two Z-buffers: one for nearest distance and one for farthest distance. It sets itself apart by bounding the ray segment for intersection calculations using these Z-buffer distances. If no Z-buffer information exists for a pixel, intersection calculations are skipped. PARC typically reduces the computation of primary rays by a factor of four [S4, unofficial].

## Operating characteristics
*   **Time Complexity:** The cost of generating the acceleration data structure (SSM) is very small compared to the total rendering time [S1, unofficial]. The method reduces ray casting time to almost a quarter of the time taken by a naive ray caster [S3, unofficial].
*   **Measured Performance:** 3 to 4 times faster when using alpha and depth tests compared to not using them [S3, unofficial].
*   **Strengths:** No CPU-side preprocessing required; leverages hardware z-occlusion culling; reduces framebuffer write operations by discarding transparent fragments [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial].
*   **Limitations:** Only skips external empty spaces; effectiveness degrades with high data dispersion [S3, unofficial]. Illumination calculation is performed on the CPU in the initial phase, limiting dynamic lighting capabilities compared to GPU-based methods like Engel, Kraus & Ertl [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The technique was introduced by Westermann & Sevenich in work [WS01] [S3, unofficial]. It is a [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) optimization that accelerates ray casting by skipping empty space intervals in the volume integral, using 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals [S3, unofficial]. Unlike Engel, Kraus & Ertl, this technique performs illumination calculation uniquely and in the initial phase on the CPU [S3, unofficial].
